description:
We are a team of 5 participants full of imagination and a desire to explore the universe. 

Our challenge in the game is based on 2 missions: a rocket that travels to the Moon or Benu. To do this, we will plan the mission, choose the parts, build the rocket, and most importantly, plan the budget so we don't spend more than we can afford. 

Our motto is: build, learn by exploring, and fly higher like a rocket heading toward the stars!
summary:
Space Construction is an educational game that turns NASA mission research into interactive simulations. The team developed two experiences with distinct scientific objectives: collecting and returning samples from the asteroid Bennu in the BRAZIOSIRIS-REx mission, and conducting a fictional helium-3 survey on the Moon in the Lunar Hedgehog mission.

In both scenarios, players select equipment, manage limited resources, and see how choices made during transit, collection, and return shape the final scientific outcome. By pairing documented NASA data and events with accessible gameplay mechanics, the game teaches planning, risk assessment, and critical decision-making.

Designed for players of all ages, these scenarios turn complex mission concepts into a playable experience with historical references.
details:
Game Details:

Mission 1: BRAZIOSIRIS-REx – Bennu Sample Return: Inspired by NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission, this simulation challenges players to collect regolith from asteroid Bennu’s loose surface without getting stuck. Starting with 100 credits, players equip up to two modules (Sampling Arm, Extra Fuel, or Precision Navigation) and progress through six phases: Launch, Approach, Touch, Decision, Return, and Lab. After sending the Send GO command, players must trigger Back away at the right moment—balancing real NASA sample mass milestones (60 g, 70.3 g, and 121.6 g) against a simulated 6.5-second stuck limit before analyzing their results in the lab.

Mission 2: Lunar Hedgehog – Helium-3 Survey: Inspired by Artemis II, Apollo 11, and NASA lunar research, this fictional crewed mission tasks players with managing power, fuel, crew safety, and data logging across six stages: Launch Prep, Radiation Alert, Far-Side Flyby, Powered Descent, Helium-3 Survey, and Return. Players equip up to three modules within a 100-credit and 720 kg mass limit (exceeding 525 kg costs extra launch fuel). Key decisions—such as managing power during radiation alerts, saving flight logs before a simulated far-side blackout, choosing a landing site, and sealing samples—determine whether the player achieves an Incomplete, Partial, or Survey Complete outcome.

Technical Details:
The game runs in the browser. HTML structures the screens, CSS defines the appearance, and JavaScript executes the mission rules, controls the timers, and calculates the outcomes of the player's choices. The AI tools served as support for development and documentation. The research, mission proposals, creative choices, and decisions regarding the game remained the responsibility of the team. Claude: assisted with writing, reviewing, and debugging the game's code. ChatGPT and Gemini: assisted with fact-checking sources, reviewing the game, and organizing the documentation, with subsequent manual review by the team. Meta AI: was used for logo creation.

Innovation Highlights:
Two missions with distinct problems: The first emphasizes the moment of collection and recoil on an asteroid; the second combines crew protection, communications, mass, energy, fuel, and the return of evidence.

Verifiable consequences: Choices are not merely narrative: they alter performance, safety, resources, and the quality of the results presented in the final report.

Research transformed into mechanics: The team's original research was adapted into engineering decisions that the player must face.

Real data and transparent rules: The experience distinguishes between historical facts, scientific goals, and invented parameters to make the simulation playable.

Learning through repetition: The player can compare strategies and understand why a mission ends in success, a partial outcome, or failure.
